Midday sun drives razor shadows across bare broken rock, the sky a committed cobalt so dark it presses down, the yellow flowers lit almost white where the light hits hardest.
A black storm wall stands over the next ridge while the meadow blazes in full amber sun, every wet petal a lit coal against the purple-black cloud behind.
Alpenglow burns pink-orange across the high snowfield while the meadow below drowns in deep blue shadow, the two colours meeting in a hard horizontal line across the slope.
Low sun rakes across the slope at five degrees, each clump of flowers throwing a long violet shadow over the loose stone, the petals themselves burning copper-orange on their lit side.
One break in grey cloud drops a single bright column of gold onto a patch of red flowers, the surrounding meadow held in cold slate, that lit patch almost aggressive in its warmth.
Backlight coming low through the petals turns them into coloured glass — magenta and gold — while the broken rock behind them sits in near-black shadow.
Cold clear early light catches white frost still locked in the shade between stones while a few inches out in the sun the flowers blaze in full saturated crimson, both states visible at once.
The sky grades from pale straw at the ridge line to deep near-violet at the top of the frame, the snow below lit the same pale straw, the two surfaces rhyming across the height.
After the shower the wet stone is almost black and mirror-bright, catching a hard orange patch of sky in its face while the flowers around it stay their own electric blue.
A rainbow stands against the retreating grey storm over the snowfield, its violet arc meeting the white surface, the near meadow still dripping, every petal holding a small silver bead.
The last gold light abandons the meadow and climbs the rock face above, the flowers already in cold blue dusk, the stone above them burning amber-orange as if on fire.
Cold blue dusk holds the whole meadow while one strip of snowfield at the far edge still catches direct sun, that stripe a hard warm ivory against everything else gone steel-blue.
Snow-bounce light floods up from a low patch of old snow and fills the shadows under the flowers from below, petals lit jade-green on their undersides by reflected cold white.
A sudden hailstorm leaves its white stones scattered bright among the purple flowers, each small sphere catching a point of silver light against the saturated violet around it.
Thin high-altitude noon sun makes the blue flowers almost ultraviolet, the shadows under each stone perfectly black with no soft edge, the air itself offering no diffusion at all.
A raking sidelight from the west catches every water-filled hollow between the stones, each pool a flat mirror of orange sky, the flowers between them in cold green shadow.
The sun passes behind a single high cloud and the meadow drops from gold to cold pewter in a second, the snow upslope still burning white, the flowers now a muted red-violet waiting.
Pre-dawn blue-violet light sits on the snowfield and the loose stone equally, the first flowers at the snow edge barely distinguishable until one catches the coming east and goes amber.
A second sun seems to rise — the snowfield above reflecting full direct light down the slope, washing the flowers in double illumination, shadows appearing from two directions at once.
Midmorning light hits the meltwater stream running across the broken rock and breaks into a thousand white splinters, the dark wet stones around it holding the stream in a black frame.
Thin cloud acts as a single enormous softbox, removing all shadows entirely, the flowers responding by becoming more saturated than in direct sun — the red impossibly red, the blue a bruise.
A cold front's leading edge turns the sky a greenish-white over the snowfield while the sun still lights the flowers in copper-yellow below, the two light temperatures fighting across the frame.
Late afternoon casts the whole slope in amber while the high snow above goes pink and the shadows between the loose stones go a saturated indigo, three colour temperatures in one frame.

The exact moment the sun clears the eastern ridge and drives the first direct ray across the frost-white loose stone, a line of warm gold advancing across cold silver as if the stone were being set alight.
A single high cirrus cloud catches the last red light of evening and throws a faint rose wash across the snowfield while the meadow below sits in the blue-grey that follows the vanished sun.
